title: Pawn Chase!
reviewNotes: Three branches, 18 exact positions from complete six-piece board. Bc5+ preserves the knight via Nb7/Nd6+, then Bd4 attacks b2 and threatens actual Bf6 mate after either ...b1=Q or ...a3. The premature Bd4 blockade loses the knight and draws. Selected source defenses only.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players will accept a draw, but only a true genius would be able to win from this position. You see black has two connected passers that are only two squares away from getting a new queen and winning the game. And it is not simple at all to stop these pawns. If we try bishop to D4, protecting the square, now after A3, black is threatening to push the pawn with the defense of the other pawn, and there is simply no way to prevent that. White's best try is to give a check to the king, pick up this pawn, and after we lose the knight, we are stopping the promotion to a new queen. But with a bishop left, there's no checkmate, so this game is going to be a draw. And the knight is just too slow to reach the pawns, even with a check. Knights are really bad at stopping pawns. There is no way to prevent the B1 square, so black is going to get a queen and win. So is this it? Does white have to accept the draw? Well, not exactly. White has a brilliant sequence that starts with bishop to C5 check. Now of course, if the king simply moves away, we're going to be able to play bishop to A3, now stopping the push of the pawn and not allowing the push of this other pawn. The king is going to march, pick up the pawns, and win the game. But of course, black can play king to E8, now gaining a precious tempo on the white knight. Remember, we cannot allow the loss of the knight or we're not going to have enough material to checkmate the black king. And again, moving this knight aimlessly is going to allow black to promote the pawn. But white finds an interesting idea. He plays knight to B7, a mysterious move. The pawn pushes, and there is simply no way to stop it. But of course, we have access to a new check, and it seems like white can at least delay the inevitable. This square is defended by the knight, and both of these squares are x-rayed by the bishop. So if the king moves to either one of them, there is going to be a discovered check, picking up the pawn, and from here it's going to be easy to win the game. But of course, the king can go to D8, and again threaten to get a queen on the next move. But here comes the final nail in this coffin. The very precise and patient bishop to d4. Believe it or not, this move is a fork. We are attacking the pawn, but if the pawn is either pushed or defended, on the next move we're going to be playing bishop to f6 with an unexpected checkmate. If you love majestic chess, follow me for more.
